summary: Written by the IAB, this document gives considerations for UNilateral Self-Address Fixing processes, where a host behind a NAT tries to learn the address others can reach it at. It lays out the problems and the conditions under which such techniques should be treated as short-term workarounds.

plainLanguage.summary: A host behind a NAT may not know which address and port another host sees. This memo explains why tricks for finding that address are unreliable and should be temporary.

questions: why are nat workarounds short term fixes
what did the iab say about nat
why are nat address discovery tricks unreliable
subtitle: Why learning an outside address from behind a NAT is only a limited, transitional workaround.

tldr.problem: A host behind one or more Network Address Translators (NATs) may not know the address and port by which a peer can reach it.
tldr.mechanism: The IAB describes the limits and risks of unilateral self-address fixing (UNSAF) and lists five issues every proposal must address.
tldr.outcome: The memo says these workarounds MUST be transitional in IETF protocols and should be deprecated when sound technical approaches become available.

today: RFC 3424 is an Informational memo published in November 2002. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Self-Address Problem
sections.content:
When one or more Network Address Translators (NATs) sit between two endpoints, the address translation is held inside the NAT. An endpoint may therefore not know the address and port that are valid from a peer's network. Unilateral Self-Address Fixing (UNSAF) describes attempts by an endpoint to discover or establish the address and port by which it is known.

A client that starts communication may create a NAT binding as a side effect. A server that only waits for incoming connections does not create one, so some mechanism would have to establish a binding before communication can start. The memo says there is no complete solution: translations can change or be reclaimed, requiring keep-alives or repeated checks.

The IAB says IETF protocols MUST treat these workarounds as transitional and intends to deprecate them when sound technical approaches are available.
sections.plainLanguage: A host behind a NAT may not know which address another host can use to reach it. A discovery trick may work only temporarily because the NAT can change or remove the address mapping.

sections.title: Why Address Discovery Has Limits
sections.content:
An UNSAF client asks a service in another address realm to report the address it sees. That report is specific to the service's place in the network. There is no single, well-defined outside of a NAT, and a different service may see a different address for the same client.

The helper service is not integrated with the NAT, so it cannot know the NAT's rules or predict when a translation will change. Connectionless traffic such as UDP can be especially affected by changing bindings. Periodic refreshes also require both the client and service to track assumed communication state, and adding a helper creates another dependency that can fail.

Without middlebox communication (MIDCOM), a workaround may let incoming traffic bypass a NAT or firewall without respecting the firewall's policies. The memo says proposals can reduce some problems by limiting address discovery to one named service and restricting the method to outbound service requests.
sections.plainLanguage: A helper reports only the address it sees, and another service may see a different one. The helper also cannot control the NAT, while bypassing the NAT can bypass firewall protections.

sections.title: Different NATs Behave Differently
sections.content:
The memo reports wide variation among deployed NATs. Some drop fragmented packets because they cannot make a mapping without complete TCP or UDP headers. Application Layer Gateways (ALGs) may inspect traffic based on port numbers, but their behavior can be undocumented or unreliable, including when data spans TCP segments or packets use TCP options.

Many NATs work more reliably with TCP than with UDP, and UDP mapping timers vary. Port assignments can change unpredictably; parallel NATs can also make the observed IP address vary. These differences make it difficult to assume that one workaround will behave consistently across networks.
sections.plainLanguage: NAT equipment does not all handle traffic the same way. A method that works on one network may fail on another, or stop working when an address mapping changes.

sections.title: What a Workaround Proposal Must Explain
sections.content:
Because UNSAF methods are short-term fixes, the IAB says every proposal must explicitly address five points:

  1. Define one precise problem and keep the proposed fix within that scope.
  2. Describe an exit strategy or transition plan.
  3. Explain how the approach could make systems more brittle, such as by adding dependencies across network layers.
  4. Identify requirements for longer-term technical solutions and contribute to finding them.
  5. Discuss the practical behavior of deployed NATs, supported by experience reports.

The memo warns that generalizing a short-term fix can prolong dependence on it and make it no longer short term.
sections.plainLanguage: A proposal must say exactly which problem it addresses, how users can move away from it, and what dependencies or NAT behaviors could cause failures. It must also help identify the needs of a longer-term solution.

sections.title: Security Considerations and Examples
sections.content:
The security concern is that, without MIDCOM, an UNSAF process cannot make a firewall admit incoming communication under proper supervision. A workaround may therefore circumvent the policy the firewall is meant to enforce, especially if one host acts for several internal machines.

Appendix C illustrates why an address can depend on the observer. In its example, Box B sees Box A at an address and port on 10.1.2.27, while Box C sees an address in 192.168.3.0/24. A second example describes a home network with separate wired and wireless private realms after a NAT-enabled wireless access point is added.
sections.plainLanguage: A workaround that opens a path through a NAT may also bypass a firewall rule. The examples show that the same host can appear at different addresses from different parts of a network.
